summary: Defines an extension to QUIC for sending and receiving unreliable datagrams over a QUIC connection. They are not retransmitted if lost, which suits real-time data. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Most QUIC messages are guaranteed to arrive. This adds postcards that may get lost, but are fast.

questions: how to send udp-like data in quic
what is the quic datagram extension
subtitle: How QUIC connections can carry application data that is sent once and never retransmitted.

tldr.problem: QUIC streams are reliable, but real-time applications often prefer data that is not retransmitted. Building that on raw UDP means a separate handshake and a separate security and congestion context.
tldr.mechanism: Two new DATAGRAM frame types (0x30 and 0x31) carry application data inside a QUIC packet with no retransmission. A max_datagram_frame_size transport parameter (0x20) tells the peer that DATAGRAM frames are accepted and how large they may be.
tldr.outcome: Unreliable data shares the connection's handshake, encryption and congestion control with reliable streams. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9221 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2022, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the DATAGRAM extension to QUIC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 9000 defines QUIC as a secure, multiplexed connection for reliable streams of application data. Each QUIC frame type defines whether the data it carries is retransmitted, and streams use STREAM frames.

Some applications, especially real-time ones, prefer unreliable delivery. They have typically built on UDP (RFC 768) and often added security with DTLS (RFC 6347). This document gives them another option: two new DATAGRAM frame types that carry application data without requiring retransmissions, inside the same QUIC connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally QUIC promises to resend anything that gets lost. This adds a way to send a note once and not worry if it goes missing.

sections.title: Why Unreliable Data Inside QUIC
sections.content:
The RFC lists three benefits over existing solutions. An application that wants both a reliable stream and an unreliable flow to the same peer can share one handshake and one authentication context, which can reduce latency compared to opening both a TLS connection and a DTLS connection. QUIC loss recovery is described as more nuanced than the DTLS handshake, so recovery can happen more quickly. And QUIC datagrams are subject to QUIC congestion control, so one controller covers reliable and unreliable data.

The text names audio/video streaming, gaming and other real-time applications as likely users. It also suggests an IP packet tunnel over QUIC, such as a VPN, where one connection carries control data on reliable streams and tunneled packets in datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: If you already have a safe road open between two houses, you can send both the important parcels and the throwaway postcards down the same road instead of building a second one.

sections.title: The max_datagram_frame_size Transport Parameter
sections.content:
Support for receiving DATAGRAM frames is advertised with the QUIC transport parameter max_datagram_frame_size (value 0x20). It is a variable-length integer giving the largest DATAGRAM frame, counting the frame type, length and payload, that the endpoint will receive, in bytes. The default is 0, meaning DATAGRAM frames are not supported. Any value above 0 means they are supported.

An endpoint MUST NOT send DATAGRAM frames until it has received this parameter with a non-zero value during the handshake (or a previous handshake, if 0-RTT is used), and MUST NOT send a frame larger than the value it received. Receiving a DATAGRAM frame without having advertised support, or one larger than the advertised limit, MUST end the connection with a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION error. For most uses the RFC recommends sending 65535, meaning any DATAGRAM frame that fits in a QUIC packet is accepted.

The limit is unidirectional, so an application protocol MAY use datagrams in only one direction. A client using 0-RTT MAY remember the server's value so it can send DATAGRAM frames in 0-RTT packets. A server that accepts 0-RTT data MUST then send a value at least as large as before, and the client MUST end the connection with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION if the new value is smaller than the stored one. Application protocols MUST define what happens when the parameter is absent, and can fail the handshake if datagrams are essential.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending postcards, each side says the biggest postcard it will accept. Zero means no postcards at all. Sending one that is too big, or when nobody said yes, is against the rules.

sections.title: The DATAGRAM Frame
sections.content:
The frame Type field has the form 0b0011000X, so it is 0x30 or 0x31. The lowest bit is the LEN bit (0x01). If it is 0, there is no Length field and the Datagram Data runs to the end of the packet. If it is 1, a Length field is present.

Length is a variable-length integer giving the size of the Datagram Data in bytes. Datagram Data holds the bytes to deliver. Empty (zero-length) datagrams are allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: A postcard has a tag saying whether the length is written on it. If not, the message just runs to the end of the envelope.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and Multiplexing
sections.content:
When an application sends a datagram, QUIC creates a DATAGRAM frame and puts it in the first available packet. The frame SHOULD be sent as soon as possible, subject to things like congestion control, and MAY be coalesced with other frames. A receiver SHOULD hand valid data to the application immediately if it can process the frame and store the contents. Like STREAM frames, DATAGRAM frames MUST be protected with 0-RTT or 1-RTT keys.

The size limit from max_datagram_frame_size can be reduced further by the max_udp_payload_size transport parameter and by the path MTU. DATAGRAM frames cannot be fragmented, so applications must cope with a smaller usable size.

DATAGRAM frames belong to the connection as a whole and carry no stream ID at the QUIC layer. Telling flows or kinds of datagrams apart is up to the application protocol. One recommended pattern is a variable-length integer at the start of the Datagram Data. QUIC implementations SHOULD offer an API to give DATAGRAM frames priorities relative to each other and to streams.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC puts your postcard in the next available truck. It will not cut a postcard in pieces, so if the truck is small, you must write shorter cards. QUIC does not label cards by topic, so your app must do that.

sections.title: Acknowledgement, Flow Control and Congestion Control
sections.content:
DATAGRAM frames are not retransmitted on loss, but they are ack-eliciting (RFC 9002). Receivers SHOULD support delaying ACK frames, within the limits of max_ack_delay, for packets containing only DATAGRAM frames, since the sender takes no action if they are briefly unacknowledged. An implementation MAY tell the application that a datagram was probably lost or was acknowledged. An acknowledgement only shows that the receiver's transport layer processed the frame, not that the application did, so it cannot replace application-level signals.

There is no flow control for DATAGRAM frames, and they count toward no data limit. Because they are unreliable, a receiver MAY drop them if it cannot process them.

DATAGRAM frames use the connection's congestion controller. The sender MUST either delay a frame until the controller allows it or drop it without sending, and MAY then notify the application. Implementations can optionally let the application set an expiration time after which a congestion-controlled frame ought to be dropped unsent.
sections.plainLanguage: Postcards are not resent, but the post office still asks for a receipt now and then. They share the road with the registered mail, so they have to wait their turn when it is busy, and a receiver that is swamped may toss some.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DATAGRAM frames have the same security properties as the rest of a QUIC connection, and the considerations of RFC 9000 apply. Like STREAM frames, all application data in DATAGRAM frames MUST be protected by 0-RTT or 1-RTT keys. Application protocols that send DATAGRAM frames in 0-RTT need a profile defining acceptable 0-RTT use (RFC 9001, Section 5.6).

An on-path adversary able to drop packets might detect use of DATAGRAM frames, because without transport-level retransmission such connections respond differently to packet loss than others.
sections.plainLanguage: Postcards ride in the same locked, sealed truck as everything else. The only giveaway is that a lost postcard is never resent, which a snoop could notice.
